It begins like a warm desert breeze and ends in a labyrinth with no clear exit, inviting you into a dreamscape painted with surgical precision by the Eagles. Every note feels intentional. The haunting chord progression in B minor constructs a sonic mirage—seductive, hypnotic, and quietly unsettling. The lyrics operate on multiple layers. On the surface, it’s a tale of luxury and entrapment. Beneath that, it becomes a meditation on American excess, fame, addiction, or whatever personal interpretation the listener brings. That’s the genius.  The twin guitar solo in the outro doesn’t simply harmonize. It ascends, weaving two distinct voices into one of the most iconic codas in rock history. It doesn’t resolve in a traditional sense. It lingers. And that’s not a flaw—it’s the design. We, like the narrator, are trapped inside the music’s walls, unable to fully leave because the experience refuses to fade.  What other song is so widely interpreted, yet so universally revered? What other track dares to leave you with more questions than answers, yet still feels whole?  Hotel California is a masterpiece not just because it was written. It’s a masterpiece because it haunts you.

Thats fake. but here is an interesting thing about video games.  Today, video games make up a $100 billion global industry, and nearly two-thirds of American homes have household members who play video games regularly. And it’s really no wonder: Video games have been around for decades and span the gamut of platforms, from arcade systems, to home consoles, to handheld consoles and mobile devices. They’re also often at the forefront of computer technology.  The Early Days Though video games are found today in homes worldwide, they actually got their start in the research labs of scientists.  In 1952, for instance, British professor A.S. Douglas created OXO, also known as noughts and crosses or a tic-tac-toe, as part of his doctoral dissertation at the University of Cambridge. And in 1958, William Higinbotham created Tennis for Two on a large analog computer and connected oscilloscope screen for the annual visitor’s day at the Brookhaven National Laboratory in Upton, New York.  In 1962, Steve Russell at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology invented Spacewar!, a computer-based space combat video game for the PDP-1 (Programmed Data Processor-1), then a cutting-edge computer mostly found at universities. It was the first video game that could be played on multiple computer installations.  Dawn of the Home Console In 1967, developers at Sanders Associates, Inc., led by Ralph Baer, invented a prototype multiplayer, multi-program video game system that could be played on a television. It was known as “The Brown Box.”  Baer, who’s sometimes referred to as Father of Video Games, licensed his device to Magnavox, which sold the system to consumers as the Odyssey, the first video game home console, in 1972. Over the next few years, the primitive Odyssey console would commercially fizzle and die out.  Yet, one of the Odyssey’s 28 games was the inspiration for Atari’s Pong, the first arcade video game, which the company released in 1972. In 1975, Atari released a home version of Pong, which was as successful as its arcade counterpart.  Magnavox, along with Sanders Associates, would eventually sue Atari for copyright infringement. Atari settled and became an Odyssey licensee; over the next 20 years, Magnavox went on to win more than $100 million in copyright lawsuits related to the Odyssey and its video game patents.  In 1977, Atari released the Atari 2600 (also known as the Video Computer System), a home console that featured joysticks and interchangeable game cartridges that played multi-colored games, effectively kicking off the second generation of the video game consoles.  The video game industry had a few notable milestones in the late 1970s and early 1980s, including:  The release of the Space Invaders arcade game in 1978  The launch of Activision, the first third-party game developer (which develops software without making consoles or arcade cabinets), in 1979  The introduction to the United States of Japan’s hugely popular Pac-Man  Nintendo’s creation of Donkey Kong, which introduced the world to the character Mario  Microsoft’s release of its first Flight Simulator game  The Video Game Crash In 1983, the North American video game industry experienced a major “crash” due to a number of factors, including an oversaturated game console market, competition from computer gaming, and a surplus of over-hyped, low-quality games, such as the infamous E.T., an Atari game based on the eponymous movie and often considered the worst game ever created.  Lasting a couple of years, the crash led to the bankruptcy of several home computer and video game console companies.  The video game home industry began to recover in 1985 when the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES), called Famicom in Japan, came to the United States. The NES had improved 8-bit graphics, colors, sound and gameplay over previous consoles.  Nintendo, a Japanese company that began as a playing card manufacturer in 1889, released a number of important video game franchises still around today, such as Super Mario Bros., The Legend of Zelda, and Metroid.  Additionally, Nintendo imposed various regulations on third-party games developed for its system, helping to combat rushed, low-quality software. Third-party developers released many other long-lasting franchises, such as Capcom’s Mega Man, Konami’s Castlevania, Square’s Final Fantasy, and Enix’s Dragon Quest (Square and Enix would later merge to form Square Enix in 2003).  In 1989, Nintendo made waves again by popularizing handheld gaming with the release of its 8-bit Game Boy video game device and the often-bundled game Tetris. Over the next 25 years, Nintendo would release a number of successful successors to the Game Boy, including the Game Boy color in 1998, Nintendo DS in 2004, and Nintendo 3DS in 2011.   The First Console War Also in 1989, Sega released its 16-bit Genesis console in North America as a successor to its 1986 Sega Master System, which failed to adequately compete against the NES.  With its technological superiority to the NES, clever marketing, and the 1991 release of the Sonic the Hedgehog game, the Genesis made significant headway against its older rival. In 1991, Nintendo released its 16-bit Super NES console in North America, launching the first real “console war.”  The early- to mid-1990s saw the release of a wealth of popular games on both consoles, including new franchises such as Street Fighter II and Mortal Kombat, a fighting game that depicted blood and gore on the Genesis version of the game.  In response to the violent game (as well as congressional hearings about violent video games), Sega created the Videogame Rating Council in 1993 to provide descriptive labeling for every game sold on a Sega home console. The council later gives rise to the industry-wide Entertainment Software Rating Board, which is still used today to rate video games based on content.  In the mid-1990s, video games leaped to the Big Screen with the release of the Super Mario Bros. live-action movie in 1993, followed by Street Fighter and Mortal Kombat over the next two years. Numerous movies based on video games have been released since.  With a much larger library of games, lower price point, and successful marketing, the Genesis had leapfrogged ahead of the SNES in North America by this time. But Sega was unable to find similar success in Japan.    Modern Age of Gaming In 2005 and 2006, Microsoft’s Xbox 360, Sony’s Playstation 3, and Nintendo’s Wii kicked off the modern age of high-definition gaming. Though the Playstation 3—the only system at the time to play Blu-rays—was successful in its own right, Sony, for the first time, faced stiff competition from its rivals.  The Xbox 360, which had similar graphics capabilities to the Playstation 3, was lauded for its online gaming ecosystem and won far more Game Critics Awards than the other platforms in 2007; it also featured the Microsoft Kinect, a state-of-the-art motion capture system that offered a different way to play video games (though the Kinect never caught on with core gamers or game developers).  And despite being technologically inferior to the other two systems, the Wii trounced its competition in sales. Its motion-sensitive remotes made gaming more active than ever before, helping it appeal to a much larger slice of the general public, including people in retirement homes.  Towards the end of the decade and beginning of the next, video games spread to social media platforms like Facebook and mobile devices like the iPhone, reaching a more casual gaming audience. Rovio, the company behind the Angry Birds mobile device game (and, later Angry Birds animated movie), reportedly made a whopping $200 million in 2012.  In 2011, Skylanders: Spyro’s Adventure brought video games into the physical world. The game required players to place plastic toy figures (sold separately) onto an accessory, which reads the toys’ NFC tags to bring the characters into the game. The next few years would see several sequels and other toy-video game hybrids, such as Disney Infinity, which features Disney characters.  The 8th generation of video games began with the release of Nintendo’s Wii U in 2012, followed by the Playstation 4 and Xbox One in 2013. Despite featuring a touch screen remote control that allowed off-TV gaming and being able to play Wii games, the Wii U was a commercial failure—the opposite of its competition—and was discontinued in 2017.  In early 2017, Nintendo released its Wii U successor, the Nintendo Switch, the only system to allow both television-based and handheld gaming. Microsoft released its 4K-ready console, the Xbox One X, in late 2017, and followed up in 2020 with the Xbox Series X and Series S. In 2020, Sony released the Playstation 5, a successor to Playstation 4.  With their new revamped consoles, both Sony and Microsoft currently have their sights set on virtual reality gaming, a technology that has the potential to change the way players experience video games.  Sources ‘Spacewar!’ The story of the world’s first digital video game. Once upon a time (back in the very early 1990's) I was a key Systems Analyst for a very very large global law firm, one which was at the very leading edge of bringing personal computing power directly into the hands of attorneys. Because of its size and because of how far in advance our projects were, this law firm was extraordinarily influential and anybody who wished to bring their products into the legal market vertical would beat a path to our door in the hope that we would adopt their technology. Believe it or not, one of those companies that came begging was none other than Google. They had an appliance that could be installed within a private network and would then scan and categorize internal document repositories and create a private search experience. Back in 1990/1991, this was revolutionary.  We installed their appliance and put it through the paces, and were impressed enough at the potential for attorneys to search the voluminous amounts of documents obtained via discovery that we put together a "smoking gun" demo for the Technology Committee. The demo rolled brilliantly. In mere seconds we were able to cull through 10's of 1000's of documents, find all the references to the most important legal consideration, and then stack rank the results. Usually, this took 1000's of man hours - not all of which were billable.  We expected the Committee attorneys to be thrilled at the potential benefits. We couldn't have been more wrong. Instead, their response was that all their education, training and experience meant that they were eminently more qualified to determine what was, and was not, legally important than some computer program which had not even ever gone to law school. They did not want a computer telling them what was the "smoking gun". They would retain ownership of that skill, thankyouverymuch.  Obviously, the project went nowhere. Google would later drop their appliance anyway. And within 10 years every attorney was more than happy to be using public search engines without any sense of irony as to how they pooh-poohed it a few years earlier. Worse, within 15 years the law firm was spending 100's of 1000's of dollars every year to scan documents, load them into an expensive proprietary database, scan and index them, and then - you guessed it - use an internal search engine to find all the "smoking guns".

16:38 One of the biggest reason why tech isn't advancing as much as in the past is what is known in the tech world as Moore's Law, formed by the co-founder of Intel, Gordon Moore, in the 60's, which states that the transistors in the microchips found in electronic devices double every two years. Right now, we're approaching the physical limits of that law and we're experiencing severe diminishing returns.   Through the generations, the way microchips have increased in performance is by reducing the size of the individual transistors, thereby enabling the increase in transistor amounts per microchip area. Ergo, smaller transistors equals more transistors and more transistors equals more power. However, you can only reduce the transistors so much.   Right now, transistors have reached atomic scale and at that scale, the movement of the electrons are about to go quantum and if you know anything about quantum mechanics, you would see why that's a problem: I don't want this to be a physics class but the laws that govern the large-scale 'world' we can observe without tools like microscopes, or what is called classical mechanics or general relativity, is very very different from the laws governing the world at the nanometer scale of atoms and electrons, or quantum mechanics.   Electrons are the vehicles used in the transmission of information in these transistors. The transistors either block (representing a zero) or allow (representing a one) the flow of these electrons. Doing this multiple times over at insane speeds (billions of times per seconds) across billions of transistors on a single chip represents what is obtainable in modern chips. If these channels that allow or block the flow of electrons reach or surpass atomic scale, each transistor will be transacting with single-line electrons per transfer and with the current laws of physics (read Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle) we can't accurately predict how this transactions will take place at such scale.   This is why you hear things like Moore's Law is dead online, because we can't physically double performance at the same rate as a few years ago  How many of the chip-producing companies are going around this is by working with "chiplets", where different parts of the processor are manufactured at different nanometer scales, as some parts of a processor don't need to be reduced in size all that much to get the same or slightly higher levels of performance, so they mix and match parts into one big SoC (System on Chip) and sell them as processors.  Some companies have taken this further with dubious marketing. You'd sometimes hear some big companies, during their tech presentations, mentioning that their chips operate on a 3nm node, or 2nm node, etc. Most times, this figure is gotten from the parts on the CPU made on that node, and even if sometimes most of the components are made on 5nm or even 10nm (lower is better. I also heard that Intel manufactures some components in 14nm nodes. Can't say for sure but I think it's higher; it might be lower), even when it's just around 1 - 20% of the entire processor that uses that lowest nanometer node, they still use that figure for show.   That's why recently a lot of chip-making companies see their products have such marginal and incremental improvements in performance. Some times, they repurpose old chips as new ones. Somehow it's not their fault but they can't say anything because they have to keep stakeholders happy. This is one of the biggest reasons why many companies, like NVIDIA, have resorted to using AI to increase their performance capabilities with technologies like DLSS. Anywhere you see "Super Sampling", or "Frame Generation" (which is the major rave right now that happened with the advent of generative AI, LLMs etc), just know that these are AI enhancements.  There's promising tech that seems likely to help or even totally solve this problem, like photonic computing (using light instead of electrons as the data vehicle), or quantum computing (which uses quantum superposition to store information, although this kind of technology won't work for most of our workloads as good as is currently obtainable but it's advantage is it's ability to perform some insane algorithms in record time). Nice thing about heat recovery units is that they are really simple technology, it is literally just a simple heat exchanger. If you were a "computer nerd" you were most likely someone who didn't really have a social life. And it was weird to just not go out and stay at home constantly looking at a screen. **Old School Computers** refer to the early generations of personal and mainframe computers that paved the way for modern computing. They are celebrated for their historical importance, unique hardware designs, and the nostalgic charm they carry for tech enthusiasts.  ---  ## 🖥️ Key Eras of Old School Computers  ### 1. **Mainframe Era (1950s–1970s)** - **Examples**: IBM 1401, UNIVAC I, PDP-11 - **Characteristics**:   - Huge machines occupying entire rooms   - Used punch cards for input   - Extremely expensive and used mainly by governments and large corporations  ---  ### 2. **Home Computer Boom (Late 1970s–1980s)** - **Examples**:   - Commodore 64   - Apple II   - Atari 800   - ZX Spectrum - **Characteristics**:   - Affordable for consumers   - Connected to TVs as monitors   - Used cassette tapes or floppy disks for storage   - Popular for programming in BASIC and playing 8-bit games  ---  ### 3. **Early IBM-Compatible PCs (1980s–early 1990s)** - **Examples**: IBM PC (1981), IBM XT, IBM AT, early clones by Compaq and Dell - **Characteristics**:   - Ran MS-DOS or early versions of Windows   - Used floppy disks and later hard drives   - Monochrome or CGA/EGA graphics   - Keyboard-centric interaction  ---  ## 🔧 Notable Hardware Features - **CRT Displays**: Bulky monitors with low resolution - **Mechanical Keyboards**: Durable and clicky - **Floppy Drives**: 5.25” and 3.5” disks were standard - **Serial & Parallel Ports**: Pre-USB connectivity for printers, mice, and modems  ---  ## 🕹️ Iconic Software & Games - **Operating Systems**: MS-DOS, CP/M, Apple DOS, AmigaOS - **Games**:   - *Pac-Man*, *Tetris*, *Prince of Persia*, *Oregon Trail* - **Productivity**:   - WordPerfect, Lotus 1-2-3, early versions of Microsoft Word  ---  ## 📚 Fun Facts - The **Commodore 64** is still the best-selling single computer model of all time. - Many old school computers are still being restored and used by hobbyists today. - BASIC (Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code) was a standard language for learning and creating games.  ---  ## 🎮 Want to Try One? There are many **emulators** online (like DOSBox, Vice for Commodore) where you can experience old school computing right in your browser.  Would you like a **visual timeline**, a **retro computer simulator**, or perhaps a **mini old school computer game** written in HTML?

Finally got an myself a QD-OLED display. Samsung Odyssey OLED G6 (240hz model on sale for $549 -- I didn't want to spend another $150+). It feels like I finally got my CRT back! Years and years using various IPS panels (secondary monitor is a VA panel. Good god the smearing/ghosting) just wasn't good enough.  The monitor I had before was an AOC 24G2 144hz display. Had some really good colors, honestly, and was a very nice 1080p display. Made me second-guess myself finally investing in the QD-OLED upgrade. But man, the difference the contrast makes. Having true blacks. The extra 100hz definitely adds some smoothness, but it's nothing like the explosive difference from 60hz to 144hz. And it's my first 1440p PC display, and yeah, it's a pretty nice improvement to image clarity.  Also, for anyone wondering about the diamond-shape subpixel arrangement in this monitor causing color-fringing on text: It's virtually unnoticeable. You really have to get close to the screen to really see it, and even then it's whatever. Text is sharply defined, and looks just fine. This was something I was worried about too considering how subpixel text anti-aliasing is aimed for square pixel RGB arrangements.  My widescreen HD CRT TV I still play my old console games on I think is what finally pushed me to bite the bullet. Driving home what I missed about my CRT PC monitor, and never really got over. Would still be nice if we had displays that could do native any any resolution like a CRT could. But, I still have faster response times (phosphor decay lasting longer than pixel switching time on OLED) and much faster framerate support. Better contrast too -- CRTs do true blacks, yes, but they do have a little bit of bleed-over in dark scenes with bright spots (some light haloing around the lit phosphors). And good quality IPS panels have had higher color accuracy than a CRT for a while, and this QD-OLED should top that pretty handily.  Also this is my first HDR monitor too. And... no, no, it's not a gimmick. I see that now. Whether games support it properly is another matter, but boy does it make a difference. Looking through a window in Resident Evil 4 Remake and seeing bright sunlight reflected off rocks and pouring into a very dark little home showcases just what kinds of contrast I've been missing out on in games. Brightness intensity, not just color intensity. Light sources actually look like... light sources. They're bright! Even sometimes hard to look at. Really drives the immersive factor and makes the display more like peering though a window, rather than a flat bed of pixels. SDR looks really flat in comparison.  I'm wondering how QDEL displays will fair in the future. They look pretty promising. Hmm... Also, I'm still angry Canon and Sony stopped development on SED and FED technology.

Conceived during the Cold War era as a response to emerging global threats, the F-22 was designed to achieve and maintain air superiority in the most contested environments. The aircraft's design and materials significantly reduce its radar cross-section, making it exceptionally difficult to detect and track by enemy radar systems. This stealth capability allows the F-22 to penetrate heavily defended airspace, gather crucial intelligence, and engage threats before being detected. Complementing its stealth is the ability to supercruise, meaning it can sustain supersonic speeds without the use of fuel-guzzling afterburners. This information superiority is crucial for making timely and effective decisions in high-threat scenarios.     Maneuverability is another key attribute of the F-22. Its sophisticated aerodynamic design, coupled with thrust-vectoring engines and an advanced fly-by-wire control system, enables it to perform exceptional maneuvers at high angles of attack and speeds. This agility makes the F-22 a formidable opponent in close-quarters combat, capable of outmaneuvering virtually any other fighter aircraft.     While primarily designed for air superiority, the F-22 also possesses a significant air-to-ground capability. Nevertheless, the F-22 has served with distinction in the U.S. Air Force since its full operational capability was achieved in 2005. It has participated in exercises and deployments worldwide, consistently demonstrating its unmatched air dominance capabilities. Although the Air Force is looking towards the Next Generation Air Dominance (NGAD) program for its future air superiority needs, the F-22 Raptor will continue to be a vital asset, with ongoing modernization efforts aimed at ensuring its relevance against evolving threats for years to come. Its legacy as a groundbreaking fighter aircraft that redefined air combat will undoubtedly endure in the annals of aviation history.

For those who don't understand: A nuclear bomb is a highly destructive weapon that derives its explosive power from nuclear reactions, either fission (splitting of atomic nuclei) or a combination of fission and fusion (joining of atomic nuclei). These reactions release an enormous amount of energy, leading to devastating explosions, intense heat, radiation, and long-term environmental and health effects.  Types of Nuclear Bombs  1. Atomic Bomb (A-Bomb): Uses nuclear fission, where heavy elements like uranium-235 or plutonium-239 are split to release energy. The bombs dropped on Hiroshima ("Little Boy") and Nagasaki ("Fat Man") in 1945 were fission bombs.   2. Hydrogen Bomb (H-Bomb): Uses both fission and fusion (the process that powers the Sun), where hydrogen isotopes fuse to form helium, releasing far greater energy than fission bombs.  These are also called thermonuclear weapons and are the most powerful type of nuclear bomb.    Effects of a Nuclear Explosion  Blast Wave: A powerful shockwave destroys buildings and infrastructure over a large area.  Thermal Radiation: Extreme heat can cause severe burns and ignite fires, leading to massive firestorms.  Ionizing Radiation: Exposure to radiation can cause radiation sickness, cancer, genetic mutations, and death.  Electromagnetic Pulse (EMP): A nuclear explosion can generate an EMP, which can disable electronic devices over vast distances.  Fallout: Radioactive particles from the explosion can contaminate air, water, and soil, leading to long-term environmental damage and health risks.   History and Global Impact  The first nuclear bomb was successfully tested on July 16, 1945 in the U.S.   during the Manhattan Project. Shortly after, nuclear weapons were used in warfare when the U.S. dropped bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, leading to Japan’s surrender and the end of World War II.  During the Cold War (1947–1991), nuclear weapons played a central role in the arms race between the U.S. and the Soviet Union, leading to the creation of thousands of nuclear warheads. The concept of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD)—where both sides had enough nuclear weapons to destroy each other—prevented direct conflict but increased global tensions.  Nuclear Arms Control and Disarmament  To prevent the spread of nuclear weapons, various international treaties and agreements have been established:  Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) – 1968: Prevents the spread of nuclear weapons and promotes disarmament.  Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) – 1996: Bans all nuclear test explosions.  Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (START): Agreements between the U.S. and Russia to reduce nuclear arsenals.   Current Threats and Concerns  Despite global efforts for disarmament, several countries still possess nuclear weapons, including the U.S., Russia, China, India, Pakistan, the U.K.,   France, Israel, and North Korea. The risk of nuclear war, terrorism, and accidental launches remains a serious global security concern.  Conclusion  Nuclear bombs are the most destructive weapons ever created, with the potential to wipe out entire cities and cause long-term damage to the planet. While they have played a role in deterrence, their existence continues to pose a major threat to global   peace and security.
